'''''Jubaea''''' is a genus of [[Arecaceae|palms]] with one species, '''''Jubaea chilensis''''', commonly known in English as the '''Chilean wine palm''' or '''Chile cocopalm''', and '''palma chilena'''<ref>{{cite web |title=Ficha de Antecedentes de Especie: ''Jubaea chilensis'' (Molina) Baill. |url=http://www.mma.gob.cl/clasificacionespecies/fichas16proceso/Jubaea_chilensis_16RCE_INICIO.pdf |access-date=2021-04-06 |publisher=Gobierno de Chile |language=es}}</ref> in Spanish. It is native to southwestern South America and is [[Endemism|endemic]] to a small area of central Chile between 32°S and 35°S in southern [[Coquimbo Region|Coquimbo]], [[Valparaíso Region|Valparaíso]], [[Santiago Metropolitan Region|Santiago]], [[O'Higgins Region|O'Higgins]], and northern [[Maule Region|Maule]] regions.

The extinct palm tree of [[Easter Island]] belonged to this genus as well. In 1991, the Easter Island palm was placed in its own genus, ''[[Paschalococos]]''.<ref>{{cite web |author=Zizka |first=Georg |date=1991 |title=Flowering Plants of Easter Island |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/235957861 |access-date=2023-07-30 |pages=64–65}}</ref> However, this has not been widely accepted.

==Growth==
In its area of natural distribution, young ''Jubaea''s tend to grow near adult specimens, preferring also sunny and vegetated sites.<ref name=GayanaBo/>

The thickest well-documented ''Jubaea'' was on the estate of J. Harrison Wright in [[Riverside, California]]. Its diameter "at shoulder height" was {{cvt|66|in|m|order=flip}}.<ref>Principes Vol. 1 # 2 (January 1957) p. 57.</ref> The largest of several specimens at the [[Adelaide Botanic Garden|Adelaide (South Australia) Botanic Garden]] in 1889 was stated to be {{cvt|6|ft|m|order=flip}} thick at the base.<ref>James H. Veitch, ''Gardener's Chronicle'', Vol. 6 (third series) (October 5, 1889)  p. 384.</ref> A hollow (but living) ''Jubaea'' in the [[Ocoa Valley]] near [[La Campana National Park]], Chile, is {{cvt|1.5|–|1.8|m}} thick at its base, with no apparent taper in the lower trunk.<ref>Chris Caradine, "A Day in Ocoa", THE PALM JOURNAL, # 143 (November 1998) p. 20 with photo.</ref> The largest individual specimen of indoor plant in the world was the ''Jubaea chilensis'' at [[Kew Gardens]], which was cut off by staff in 2014 because it grew to the top of its greenhouse.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Growingontheedge.net – View topic – Jubaea chilensis |url=http://www.growingontheedge.net/viewtopic.php?p=89398 |website=Growingontheedge.net |access-date=2017-04-02 |archive-date=2023-07-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230723093711/https://www.growingontheedge.net/viewtopic.php?p=89398 }}</ref> Of the more than 2,600 known species of palms, ''Jubaea chilensis'' is the second most massive, exceeded only by the floodplain or river bottom variety of ''[[Borassus aethiopum]]''.<ref>Dr. Al C. Carder, ''GIANT TREES OF WESTERN AMERICA AND THE WORLD'', (Madeira Park, British Columbia, Canada: Harbour Publishing, 2005) p. 130.</ref> Karsten and Schenck reported a maximum height of {{cvt|34|m|ft|0}} for ''Jubaea''.<ref>{{cite book | last1= Karsten | first1= Georg | last2= Schenck | first2= Heinrich | date= 1908 | title= Vegetationsbilder - Volume 6 | location= Jena, Germany | page= Plate 47 with text}}</ref>

==Uses==
The leaves can be used to weave baskets, and it has edible seeds, widely eaten and known as [[Coquito nuts]]. The sap can be used to make [[palm wine]] and [[palm syrup]], although, unlike other palms which can be tapped, the whole tree has to be felled; this is now restricted by legal protection.<ref name="kew">{{cite web |author=<!--Not stated--> |date= |title=Jubaea chilensis – Chilean wine palm |url=https://temperate.house/plant/chilean-wine-palm/ |access-date=17 October 2021 |website=www.kew.org |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |archive-date=23 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211023224353/https://temperate.house/plant/chilean-wine-palm/ }}</ref>

==Conservation==

The species is partially protected within Chile, although pressures of [[human population growth]] and expansion of grazing areas have reduced the population of the Chilean wine palm in recent centuries.<ref>C. Michael Hogan. 2008</ref> The collection of its seed and their predation by [[common degu]] may also have a negative impact on the growth of new generations of ''Jubea''.<ref name=GayanaBo>{{Cite journal |title=Regeneración natural y patrones de distribución espacial de la palma chilena Jubaea chilensis (Molina) Baillon en los bosques mediterráneos de Chile central |journal=[[Gayana. Botánica]] |last1=Miranda |first1=Alejandro |issue=1 |volume=73 |last2=Hernández |first2=H. Jaime |last3=Bustamante |first3=Ramiro |last4=Díaz |first4=E. Matías |last5=González |first5=L. Alberto |last6=Altamirano |first6=Adison |year=2016 |pages=54–63 |language=Spanish |trans-title=Natural regeneration and spatial distribution patterns of Chilean palm Jubaea chilensis (Molina) Baillon in Mediterranean forests of Central Chile|doi=10.4067/S0717-66432016000100007   |doi-access=free |url=http://www.scielo.cl/pdf/gbot/v73n1/07.pdf }}</ref> The [[IUCN Red List]] considers the palm [[Endangered]]. In August 2026, the Council of Ministers for Sustainability and Climate Change of Chile included the Chilean palm in Appendix I of the [[Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora]], the highest level of protection, restricting the palm's international trade to non-commercial purposes.<ref>{{cite web |title=Consejo de Ministros aprueba reforzar protección de la palma chilena y otras especies amenazadas contra el comercio internacional |url=https://mma.gob.cl/consejo-de-ministros-aprueba-reforzar-proteccion-de-la-palma-chilena-y-otras-especies-amenazadas-contra-el-comercio-internacional/ |website=[[Ministry for the Environment (Chile)]] |access-date=18 August 2026 |language=es |date=17 August 2026}}</ref>

A recent study concluded that predation of the fruits by humans, the seeds by the exotic rat (''[[Black rat|Rattus rattus]]'') and the young seedlings by exotic rabbits is leading to seed dispersal collapse of this species, leaving it at risk of extinction in its natural habitat.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cordero |first1=Sebastián |last2=Gálvez |first2=Francisca |last3=Fontúrbel |first3=Francisco E. |date=2021 |title=Multiple Anthropogenic Pressures Lead to Seed Dispersal Collapse of the Southernmost Palm Jubaea chilensis |journal=Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution |volume=9 |article-number=719566 |doi=10.3389/fevo.2021.719566 |issn=2296-701X|doi-access=free }}</ref> Fruit harvesting by people is shown to be unsustainable and is also a major threat to this endangered species.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cordero |first=Sebastián |last2=Gálvez |first2=Francisca |last3=Arriagada‐Honores |first3=Marisol |last4=Garrido |first4=Andrés Jesús |last5=Paredes‐Muñoz |first5=Daniela |last6=Fuentes‐Valdés |first6=Bastián |last7=Torres‐Cifuentes |first7=Fernanda |last8=Fontúrbel |first8=Francisco E. |date=2026-04-09 |title=From traditional practice to unsustainable exploitation: Fruit overharvesting on the endangered relict palm Jubaea chilensis |url=https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q139603285 |journal=Plants People Planet |doi=10.1002/PPP3.70210|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Analysis of tooth residue of the extinct [[gomphothere]] (elephant relative) ''[[Notiomastodon|Notiomastodon platensis]],'' which became extinct around 12,000 years ago as part of the [[Late Pleistocene extinctions|end-Pleistocene extinction event]], found that it consumed Chilean wine palm fruit and probably acted as a seed disperser for the species, suggesting that the dispersal ability of Chilean wine palm had already been impacted prior to modern times.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=González-Guarda |first1=Erwin |last2=Loayza |first2=Andrea P. |last3=Segovia |first3=Ricardo A. |last4=Rivals |first4=Florent |last5=Petermann-Pichincura |first5=Alia |last6=Ramírez-Pedraza |first6=Iván |last7=Asevedo |first7=Lidiane |last8=Tornero |first8=Carlos |last9=Labarca |first9=Rafael |last10=Latorre |first10=Claudio |date=2025-06-13 |title=Fossil evidence of proboscidean frugivory and its lasting impact on South American ecosystems |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41559-025-02713-8 |journal=Nature Ecology & Evolution |language=en |volume=9 |issue=7 |pages=1168–1178 |doi=10.1038/s41559-025-02713-8 |pmid=40514571 |issn=2397-334X |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The species was originally described as ''Palma chilensis'' by Chilean botanist [[Juan Ignacio Molina]] in 1808.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Molina |first1=Giovanni Ignazio |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/45304682 |title=The geographical, natural and civil history of Chili |last2=Molina |first2=Giovanni Ignazio |last3=Alsop |first3=Richard |last4=Ercilla y Zúñiga |first4=Alonso de |last5=Hayley |first5=William |last6=Boyd |first6=Henry |date=1808 |publisher=Printed for I. Riley |volume=v.1 (1808) |location=Middletown (Conn.)}}</ref> After being moved to other genera including ''[[Molinaea]], Micrococos'' and ''[[Coconut|Cocos]]'' by other botanists'','' it was finally placed in the genus ''Jubaea'' by French botanist [[Henri Ernest Baillon]] in 1895, as ''J. chilensis'' (Molina) Baill.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jubaea chilensis Baill. |url=https://worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0000220212 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230308081327/http://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0000220212 |archive-date=2023-03-08 |access-date=2025-05-01 |website=worldfloraonline.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Baillon |first1=H. |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/29644936 |title=Histoire des plantes |last2=Baillon |first2=H. |date=1895 |publisher=Librairie Hachette |volume=v. 13 |location=Paris}}</ref> 

''Jubaea'' is named after [[Juba II|King Juba II]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Canberra |first=National Arboretum |date=2020-07-03 |title=Forest 26 - Chilean Wine Palm |url=https://www.nationalarboretum.act.gov.au/living-collections/forests-and-trees/forest-26 |access-date=2025-05-01 |website=www.nationalarboretum.act.gov.au |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Kew">{{cite web |title=Chilean wine palm |url=https://temperate.house/plant/chilean-wine-palm/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211023224353/https://temperate.house/plant/chilean-wine-palm/ |archive-date=23 October 2021 |access-date=2 October 2022 |website=Temperate House, Kew Gardens |publisher=Board of Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Briones |first1=Julià Molero |last2=Pereira |first2=Trinidad Arcos |last3=Carrasco |first3=María Dolores García de Paso |last4=Reyes-Betancort |first4=Jorge Alfredo |last5=Santos-Guerra |first5=Arnoldo |last6=Jestrow |first6=Brett |last7=Francisco-Ortega |first7=Javier |date=2025-04-30 |title=On the Macaronesian endemic woody spurge Euphorbia regis-jubae Webb & Berthel. and eponyms honouring the Numidian King Juba II (48 BCE –23/24 CE) |url=https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q134297198 |journal=Curtis's Botanical Magazine |volume=42 |pages=119–133 |doi=10.1111/CURT.12623|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

==History==
[[Charles Darwin]] examined these trees on visiting Chile in 1832 on the [[Second voyage of HMS Beagle|second voyage of HMS ''Beagle'']] and noted:
{{Blockquote|text=These palms are, for their family, ugly trees. Their trunk is very large, and of a curious form, being thicker in the middle than at the base or top.<ref name="kew"/>|author=Charles Darwin}}
In 1843, a specimen was grown from seed at [[Kew Gardens]], London, England, and was moved into the [[Kew Gardens#The Temperate House|Temperate House]] in 1863, eventually growing to {{convert|19|m}}. It was believed to be the world's tallest indoor plant, until it had to be felled in 2013 because it had outgrown the space available and could not be moved. It has been replaced by seedlings from the original tree.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pumpkinbeth.com/2018/05/scott-taylor-temperate-house-supervisor/ |title=Scott Taylor, Temperate House Supervisor |last=Otway |first=Beth |date=10 May 2018 |website=www.pumpkinbeth.com |access-date=17 October 2021}}</ref>
